newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish anti-Islamist alliance takes shape.
newsitem.headline: Turkish anti-Islamist alliance takes shape.

text.p: A Turkish secularist government began to take shape on Thursday, although it still lacked the parliamentary strength needed to prevent pro-Islamist opponents killing it off at birth.
Prime minister-designate Mesut Yilmaz said he had appointed a staunchly anti-Islamist politician as his deputy and had received presidential backing for his left-right alliance.

"The president told me he would approve a government with the support of four parties," he told a news conference. Motherland Party leader Yilmaz has the backing of three other party leaders for his coalition.
Yilmaz is to present a cabinet list next week to President Suleyman Demirel, who has to approve it for Yilmaz to go to a confidence vote in parliament.
However, a partnership between outgoing prime minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamists and conservative Tansu Ciller has more MPs in the 550-seat assembly and demands power for itself.

Main opposition leader Yilmaz said he had asked Bulent Ecevit, fiercely secularist head of the Democratic Left Party, to be deputy prime minister if his coalition comes to power. "Mr Ecevit has accepted," he said.

Political instability has plagued Turkey for more than a year. Islamist Erbakan resigned as prime minister last week after months of army pressure that verged on threats to use military force against Islamist supporters.
NATO member Turkey's secularists fear the Islam-based Welfare Party's promises to increase the role of religion in public life mask a bid to create an Islamic state, like Iran.
The top brass gave Erbakan little chance to carry out pledges to forge close ties with Turkey's Moslem neighbours while he was in office.
The army expanded its ties with Israel, ignoring protests from Erbakan supporters and much of the Arab world. Ankara has a wideranging military training pact with the Jewish state.
Syria, Egypt and six Gulf Arab states on Thursday expressed deep concern over Turkish-Israeli military and security ties in a statement after talks in Syria.
The Arab countries said the cooperation "constitutes a threat to the security of Arab countries and to stability in the Middle East".

Military officials said on Thursday that Turkey had pulled most of its troops out of northern Iraq after a six-week operation against Kurdish rebels. Frequent cross-border drives into Iraq are another source of friction with the Arabs.
Turkey's powerful generals see themselves as the guardians of secularism and oppose any attempt to keep Welfare in office.

An anti-Islamist MP joined Yilmaz from Ciller's True Path Party on Thursday. But the secularist group still needs another six defections to be near winning the confidence vote, expected within two weeks.
"Everyone must play a role in protecting the secular, democratic state at this time," the defector, Isilay Saygin, said in a statement.
She was the third MP to abandon her party in under a week in anger at an attempt by the Islamists to return to power in a partnership led by Ciller.

Other former Ciller MPs upset at her ties to the Islamists have become independents or joined a conservative faction that supports Yilmaz. A group of rebel backbenchers inside True Path, say they might abstain in the confidence vote, and help Yilmaz.
